subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN SHIPPING OF UNITED STATES SUBSIDY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. What will be the effect on Canadian great lakes shipping of the order of the United States maritime administration announced today making United States ship operators on the great lakes eligible for government subsidies?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSPORT
subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN SHIPPING OF UNITED STATES SUBSIDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only to serve as the basis of an opinion the account which appeared in the Montreal Gazette this morning. I have not seen the text of the announcement made yesterday by the United States maritime administration but I understand from the press dispatch that the administration has declared the ocean route between United States lake ports and western Europe to be essential to United States trade and economy so that, I understand, they could make subsidies available to operators over that route.
However, I should like to point out to the hon. member that this seems to apply only to ocean shipping covering the route between United States lake ports and, I think, western Atlantic ports in Europe. I do not think one may infer from the communique that it is intended to subsidize operations within the great lakes themselves.

maintopic: TRANSPORT
subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN SHIPPING OF UNITED STATES SUBSIDY
speechtext: Will Canadian shipping be given any assistance of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: TRANSPORT
subtopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN SHIPPING OF UNITED STATES SUBSIDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the moment there is no Canadian shipping that is using this particular route because, as my hon. friend knows, the canals limit the oceangoing vessels to those having a draught of 14 feet or less. As the vessels on Canadian register and vessels on United Kingdom register owned by Canadian interests are all of greater draught, the question of subsidy to them does not arise at the present time.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM    INQUIRY AS TO PLANS MADE AT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister what plans, if any, were made at the recent conference with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs of that country with reference to trade between Canada and the United Kingdom?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM    INQUIRY AS TO PLANS MADE AT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman realizes, as we realized before, during and after our conversations with the Prime Minister and minister of foreign affairs of the United Kingdom, that they are as anxious as we are to increase the volume of trade between our two countries. However, that has to be a two-way traffic, and we discussed various ways in which that was being encouraged and the fact that those steps were developing at the present time an increase in that trade.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM    INQUIRY AS TO PLANS MADE AT CONFERENCE
speechtext: Could the Prime Minister be specific as to what particular means are in contemplation in relation to that trade?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED KINGDOM    INQUIRY AS TO PLANS MADE AT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows that they are both free enterprise countries and that it is the individual traders in those countries who make their own investigations and try to serve in the best way they can their own individual interests.
We were informed that there would be substantial advantage to the United Kingdom and to ourselves if more special industrial groups could visit the United Kingdom, because it was pointed out to us that it was only the very largest of their trading firms who could come here and seek markets for the commodities they have available. It was also pointed out that two or three of these groups had visited the United Kingdom and as a result of their visits there had already been a noticeable improvement in the quantity of exports they found it was possible for them to absorb from that source.

Inquiries of the Ministry
We are as much concerned as the hon. member is with the imbalance in our trade with the United Kingdom, and to the extent to which we can influence those events we would like to see as much of the needs of our economy as can be absorbed supplied from an area which would in return be only too happy to purchase more of our products.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: REPORTED DELIVERY OF ARMS BY RUSSIA IN RETURN FOR SLAVES
speechtext:
I should like to answer a question addressed to me the other day by the Leader of the Opposition when he asked:
Can he enlighten us further or indicate the position taken by this government in regard to the shocking facts disclosed in a report to Dag Hammarskjold referred yesterday to the United Nations in connection with the reported purchase of arms from Russia by the delivery of 1,500,000 Chinese slaves.
The allegations to which reference is made are to be found in the joint report on forced labour submitted to the economic and social council by the Secretary General of the United Nations and the director general of the international labour office. This document- a voluminous one-records new information on systems of forced labour submitted by member states and non-governmental organizations in accordance with a resolution of the council. It includes a report from the Chinese nationalist government entitled "Information on Forced Labour in Communist China".
This report-that is, the report from the nationalist Chinese government-is based on statements in Chinese communist newspapers of individual prisoners who had got out of China, and on Chinese communist laws and regulations. The particular reference of

my hon. friend to the purchase of arms by China to be paid for by the forced labour of Chinese is from a Hong Kong newspaper which published a letter from a Chinese in Thailand who had escaped from a prison camp in China where he had heard that this arrangement had been made.
Canada has already made its position clear at the United Nations with respect to forced labour. We have fully endorsed the condemnations by the economic and social council and the general assembly of the United Nations of the existence of systems of forced labour; we have also expressed support for the adoption of a convention on the abolition of forced labour as a means of political coercion or economic development.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for shortterm credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain; to provide also that the governor in council may extend the application of the act to cover loans made before the 1st day of June, 1957; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the act be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a representative in this house from a constituency located in the heart of the world's finest wheat growing area, I feel it my duty to place before the
Grain
committee some of the reasons I am opposing the legislation presently under consideration.
In opposing this measure I do so first of all because I feel it fails to meet the legitimate requests of the preponderance of spokesmen for western agriculture, who have on many occasions indicated their insistence on cash advances rather than bank loans. I think the excuse offered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there was not perhaps complete unanimity when the delegation recently made certain proposals to the cabinet is a mighty poor excuse for the government's refusal to meet the requests of the vast majority of the spokesmen for western agriculture.
On this point, I have been somewhat surprised at the silence of private members on the government side of the house, and I was particularly surprised at the failure of private members from the province of Saskatchewan on the government side of the house to put forth their reasons for supporting this resolution.
On occasions we in this section of the house have been asked by some of the hon. members from Saskatchewan on the government side who asked us to take a particular stand and who asked us to vote against a particular measure. I should like to ask them this question. Whom are they representing in this house when they support a proposition which has not met with the approval of a single agricultural group in the province of Saskatchewan? We are on record as being opposed to this proposal, and have asked for something worth while. The silence of private members from Saskatchewan on the Liberal side of the house in relation to this matter reveals only too clearly that they are aware of the situation, and they dare not stand up in the house and state their reasons for supporting this resolution.

This would lead us to believe that not only did our Liberal members in this house toe the line but that the Liberal party, as it has in the past, still exercises dominant control over the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan. When the Liberal leader makes a statement that is found unpalatable to his colleagues in Ottawa he is told to keep quiet and say no more about it. I do not think anyone in the province has summed up the situation more ably than the Liberal leader. It is too bad he could not have stuck to his guns and defied the powers in Ottawa.
One of the chief objections to this legislation is that it locks the door to worth-while legislation. We had this type of legislation in 1951, and it failed to satisfy the needs at that time. We are trying to establish a principle of cash advances. Members of the C.C.F. group have been talking about cash advances for over 10 years. We want that principle definitely established. The idea of treating the farmers in the manner outlined in this resolution is far from satisfactory, and we feel that the withdrawal of this legislation would enable the government to bring in legislation more in keeping with the needs of western agriculture.
I suggest that the legislation is only as good as the excuses offered on its behalf by its apologists. I have been trying to find out the reasons behind the government's insistence on this legislation. We have been told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that delegations from western Canada have asked for it. That is not true. In order to save the Liberal government some embarrassment an individual might have taken a position contrary to the vast majority of the spokemen for western agriculture, but surely the minister cannot insist on complete unanimity. Surely he will accept the wishes of at least 95 per cent of the spokesmen. I would say that as far as the grass roots are concerned it is 100 per cent. If you can find among the vast number of spokesmen representing agricultural groups in the west one or two who, to save the

government some embarrassment might be prepared to support bank loans, that is a far cry from saying there is support for this legislation on the prairies.
We even had the hon. member for Rosthern reading into the record a resolution passed at a Saskatchewan conference, completely twisting the meaning of that resolution beyond recognition in a vague and clumsy effort to prove that black is white or that white is black. When they ask for cash advances, he interprets that to mean bank loans.
Then, of course the more tortuous argument is put forth that the government are out to protect the wheat board, that somehow or other those advocating cash advances are in some way undermining the position of the wheat board. The whole validity, or lack of it, of this argument will depend upon the Liberal record with regard to that board. It seems passing strange that at this time the Liberals should be proclaiming themselves as champions of the wheat board. I suggest that one look at the record.
It is well known, as far as the C.C.F. is concerned, that long before the C.C.F. was formed the forerunners of the C.C.F., the men and women who worked in the farm movements on the prairies and who brought forth the C.C.F., these spokesmen for the farmers and workers throughout Canada were the people who gave the impetus and leadership to the creation of the wheat board. The demand was there.
As far as the Liberals are concerned, the wheat board as we know it came into being in 1935 and was brought in by the Bennett government. At the time that legislation was brought in the Liberal party fought it tooth and nail, and the leading opponent of it at that time was the late Hon. J. L. Ralston, in an eleventh hour effort to weaken, if not destroy, the wheat board. Amendments were brought in which would have the effect of placing the wheat board in operation for one year, to be extended only under certain circumstances, whereas the act brought in the wheat board on a permanent basis.
After the Liberal party had fought a losing battle to prevent the creation of the wheat board, and had used every method in its power to weaken it in order to destroy it later, it had the temerity in western Canada in 1935 to go around the country professing to be the friend of the wheat board. The late Mr. King went out to western Canada and referred to the wheat board as the brain child of the Liberal party, after his colleagues had bitterly opposed it just a few months previously. Western Liberals were elected by paying lip service to the wheat board.
Grain
What is the sorry record? We know the first step, of course, was to dismiss Mr. McFarland and the advisory committee of the wheat board, thus destroying the one vestige of producer representation on the board. I should mention in passing that later on, at a byelection in which the present Minister of Agriculture entered this house as Minister of Agriculture, the C.C.F. opposed him-unsuccessfully, of course. We opposed him because we had every reason to believe that from his record the Minister of Agriculture was opposed to the wheat board in principle, and opposed to the whole question of setting an initial price. He was opposed to the whole idea of orderly marketing. We were afraid that once in office he would join with his colleagues in Ottawa in a systematic effort to sabotage the wheat board, and that is precisely what they did.
My leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, referred to a speech made in this house by the late Mr. Motherwell, who at that time was the member for Melville, in which Mr. Motherwell denounced the Liberal government and denounced his own colleagues for seeking to destroy the wheat board. It appeared quite definite that among the vast number of Liberals who sought election in 1935 and were elected by paying lip service to the wheat board, there was at least one Liberal who stood by his convictions, and that man was the late Mr. Motherwell.
Not only did he indict the government for its attitude toward the wheat board, but he had some caustic comments to make with regard to their government by order in council. I believe he suggested that they might just as well have Mussolini take over the house, when they were governing by order in council. They had an act of parliament set forth certain procedures by which farmers could deliver their grain to the wheat board, and the government of the day-a Liberal government-sought to destroy the wheat board through underhand methods by order in council. We know that during those years of 1936-37 and 1937-38, at the time the order in council was passed to the effect that the wheat board was only to accept delivery of wheat if the price of wheat dropped below 90 cents, farmers were denied the right to deliver their wheat to the wheat board. They delivered their wheat to the elevators at prices ranging between 90 cents and $1.
Later in the same year they saw the price of wheat go up to $1.43. If the wheat board had been in operation, if the farmers had been permitted to deliver their wheat to the wheat board, they would have shared in that price through participation certificates, but the

Mr. Chairman, I must say that my treatment of this subject was occasioned by the fact, as I pointed out, that the whole basis of the argument made by some of the apologists for the resolution was their supposed concern for the wheat board. Therefore I think the validity of this argument will hinge to a very large extent upon the government's handling of the matter throughout the years, because after all the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce are two of the men who were vitally concerned with this matter at the time the wheat board was dealt with in the manner I have just been describing.
However, I will hurry on and dispose of the subject by making one further reference. Notwithstanding the indirect pressure against the wheat board in 1939, on February 16, 1939, the Minister of Agriculture announced a new wheat policy at the time the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were before the house. The pertinent point in the new policy enunciated by the government was as follows:
That the government should remain out of the grain trade and our wheat should be marketed by means of the futures market system.

Certainly under those circumstances it is quite easy to assess the validity of the arguments these hon. members have been making. Under these circumstances you may say, why have we a wheat board today? That is a proper question. It was not because of the Liberal party but in spite of them. It was because of the wave of protest that spread throughout western Canada. The United farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section; the Saskatchewan wheat pool; the Manitoba pool; the Alberta pool, all the farm organizations joined together to protest the onslaught on the wheat board. A petition was circulated throughout my province and I believe there were somewhere in the neighbourhood of 160,000 signatures on it.
At that time the Liberal government were a little more sensitive to public opinion. They had only been in office for about three years. Now they have been in office so long that they just do not care about public opinion and are prepared to ram this thing through regardless of what the people back home think. It indicates the change in the attitude of the government in recent years. At least at that time they were sensitive enough to public opinion that they made up their minds that if you could not beat it you might as well join it. The Liberal protestations of devotion to the wheat board today bear all the earmarks of a shotgun marriage, because nothing in their past has indicated that their concern about the wheat board is their real reason for bringing forward this legislation at the present time.
I have been quite interested, Mr. Chairman, in the attitude taken by other opposition groups with regard to this resolution, particularly the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party. In spite of the critical comments they have made about the measure they have announced through their leader that they intend to support the government. The same applies to the spokesman for the Social Credit group, who announced the support of his group for the legislation introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I had hoped that as a result of this discussion we might persuade the other opposition groups to join us in presenting the attitude of western agriculturists toward the resolution now before the house.

The right hon. gentleman is sometimes extremely loquacious, but on these occasions he either spoke far too much or else far too little. As reported at page 861 of Hansard he said:
. . . financing on loans has never been the best way for the farmers of western Canada.
We who come from western Canada know that it is not a good way for farmers to finance. But if that is so, and if my hon. friend knows it is so, why is he supporting

this legislation the purpose of which is financing farmers by means of loans? My right hon. friend has told the house that he has been through Saskatchewan talking at meetings here and there; but apparently he is not yet convinced that the great majority of the farmers are opposed to this legislation.
I do not know what sort of farm groups he was speaking to. I know that I met with some in Manitoba who were strongly opposed to this legislation. Perhaps the minister never came across those farmers. I come from an urban constituency; and coming as I do from an urban constituency I know that the welfare of my constituency depends upon the welfare of the farmers, and that what is good for the farmers is good for my constituency and for Canada. Members of parliament from eastern Canada also ought to realize that fact, especially those from industrial areas where farm implements have been sold in the past to western Canada. They know the unemployment which prevails in these industries because the farmers have no cash with which to buy implements. We have to get cash into the hands of the farmers, and this legislation is not designed to do it. The Minister of Agriculture must know it is not designed to do that. Yet despite the fact that he says that the financing of farmers by loans is a bad thing, apparently he still intends in this house to support it.

1 was told at that meeting that in that district 30 per cent of the wheat on the farm is already pledged.
I went on:
The reason such a large percentage of that wheat has already been pledged is that heavy costs were incurred in the production of the wheat. Farmers were obliged to get bank loans to meet those costs, md they were obliged to charge bills with machine companies, stores and oil companies, and those pills exist at the present time.
I am talking about bills owing at stores.
: am certainly not talking about liens. The ion. member for Rosthern knows the pract-ce in the west as well as I do. He knows

it is the practice during the summer, when the farmer is short of cash, for him to go to the local storekeeper or the local machine man, or to the oil dealer, and point out to the merchant that he has not enough money to pay for his stores or his supplies, and he asks the storekeeper to advance him these goods on credit and promises- here is where the pledge comes in-that when he threshes his crop he will pay that bill. There is no legal document of any kind signed; there is no lien signed; there is nothing transacted legally that compels that farmer to pay that bill when he sells his wheat. It is merely a promise he makes to the storekeeper, and the storekeeper knows from experience that the majority of farmers who make a promise of that kind will honour it.
Therefore, if the farmer received an advance on his wheat, what would he do? As soon as he got an advance he would immediately go around town and to the best of his ability pay the storekeepers the amounts he owed them. If the advance had been made at 50 per cent of the delivery, then half of the advance would be repaid and the other half would be used by the farmer to pay off any further bills he had not been able to pay when he first got the advance.
That is what I meant by the pledge. It is exactly the same as the Minister of Agriculture meant when he said the farmers would get an advance of credit from storekeepers, that in many cases the storekeepers were actually acting as the farmers' bankers. I was not suggesting that the farmer signs any note or legal contract which would have priority on an advance or a loan made by the wheat board or by the government.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer, and that is the statement made by the hon. member for Regina City. He referred to the fact that the members of the Conservative and Social Credit parties were supporting this legislation, and he implied that we were not acting in the interests of the farmers by so voting. Personally I feel that when we vote we are not voting in the interests of the C.C.F. party; we are voting that way because we believe it will be in the interests of the farmers to support this resolution.
If we had the alternative of voting either for this legislation or advances, unquestionably we would vote for advances, but we have not that chance. There is only one piece of legislation before us. We have no assurance whatsoever that if this legislation is turned down other legislation granting advances to farmers will be passed. We have

no reason to believe that, and so we are bound to ask ourselves this question. Would it be in the interests of the farmers today for the government to withdraw the legislation now before us? Would it be in the interests of the farmers for the government or the banks to stop making loans to the farmers? I am satisfied the farmers would not want that done at the present time. True, they would prefer advances, but if they cannot get advances they want loans.
I am not in any doubt about the attitude of the farmers in my constituency toward this question, because that whole matter was threshed out for a number of hours at meetings I attended last fall. At the largest meeting, held at Morrin, a meeting attended by farmers from Drumheller to Stettler and from Three Hills to Hanna, this question of government policy which had been brought to their attention at that time came up for discussion. Most of the farmers spoke quite bitterly against it.
Then the proposition was raised as to whether they should vote against the proposal and take a definite stand that they would not accept it. Much consideration was given to that question. The decision arrived at by those farmers was that they would like advances but if they could not get advances then they wanted bank loans. I was present at that meeting, and I was instructed by the farmers at that meeting to support this legislation if there was no other alternative. As I say, there is no other alternative at the present time.
What has been the attitude of the Alberta wheat pool on this question? At the last annual convention it adopted a 12-point program. In that whole program there was no mention of advances or loans. But during the conference there was mention of this question. The official wheat pool budget has this to say:
Delegates felt that advances on grain, whether interest free or otherwise, were only an emergency measure and would offer no solution to marketing problems. They believe that farmers who find it necessary to borrow should get as favourable interest rates as possible, but they did not ask that the wheat board become involved in the loaning business for fear of jeopardizing its usefulness as a merchandising agency.
They have not much faith in loans or advances as a solution to their problems, but they feel that if loans are made they should be secured at the lowest interest rate possible. That has been our main criticism of the bank loan, namely that the rate of interest is too high and should be 3J per cent. We have felt that instead of the government bringing down a policy under which the farmers can get bank loans, they should have brought down a policy under which advances

could be made to the farmers who have grain in storage by the government itself without any interest, in other words a prepayment. The government could take ownership of the wheat. It could make an initial payment, and the balance could be paid when the wheat is sold. That is the policy the farmers believe in, but the government refuses to bring down that policy. The farmers say that if they cannot get that they would be glad to get the bank loans.
Many farmers today need help of some kind or another. We in this group make no apology for supporting this legislation. We are sorry we have to support it rather than advances, but the government controls the matter. They refuse to bring down advances, and we are certainly not going to vote against the farmers receiving this small help.
I received two petitions yesterday sent by farmers in my constituency. One is from the farmers' union and contains this clause:

although I do not know-on this measure in its first stage. I think most members in the C.C.F. party from the prairies have now spoken twice.

I just wish to say another word or two and then I am finished. I want to mention the treatment this matter has received from the hon. member for Rosthern. The hon. member mentioned two main points with which I take issue. In the first place, he made the statement that this legislation is in fact what the farmers requested. After all that has been put on Hansard in the last few days I do not think I need to say much about that. I have the resolutions here. I attended the Saskatoon conference for three full days; except for my meals I was never out of the room. I know what went on there. I know not only the letter of what happened at that Saskatoon conference, but I know the spirit. I know what the people meant. I know them personally. I know what they were thinking. There is not much good going into that. If
anyone wants me to do so, I can read resolutions here by the dozen. They mention advance payments, and advance payments through the wheat board. They do not mention advance loans guaranteed by the banks or by the government.
You know, the hon. member for Rosthern is not the only one who has adopted that argument. The policy of the Saskatchewan wheat pools-
They tell Mr. McDonald.

Well, I have already said a word or two in regard to that, and I do not think I shall repeat it. We do not believe this will be permanent legislation on the statute books, and we think, that being the case, that to put it on the books now would stand in the way of better legislation, legislation which the farmers want, namely a system of advance payments on stored grain and not loans.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I only rise to ask a question arising out of the minister's statement concerning section 88 of the Bank Act. maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is just wheat.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

(Mr. Knight.)

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to make any remark except to indicate the position our party takes and why it has taken it. Since reference has been made by an hon. member of the C.C.F. party who just spoke a few minutes ago about the position of our party in this matter, I think I should make it quite clear.
We indicated at the outset that we did not believe this legislation is legislation which will meet the very urgent situation with which the farmers are confronted. We have put forward arguments which we hoped would still, at this stage, convince the government that they should adopt a system of cash payments on farm-stored grain with payments on the quota book. We have emphasized that position and we repeat it now. Nevertheless, following well established traditions, we say we will vote for a measure which certainly does not carry out what we would like to see carried out, but which at least does offer some assistance.
We still urge the government, independently of this legislation, to adopt the proposal we have made for cash payments on farm-stored grain. We have made it clear that this is a straight cash payment on the quota book, just as though the grain were delivered. We have made it clear that this is a payment without interest, because it is cash being given to the farmer for his grain, which is only being held up because it cannot be taken by the elevators.
This measure is separate and independent of that proposal. By supporting this legislation, inadequate though it may be, unsatisfactory in many respects though it may be, there will be placed on the statute books a provision under which farmers can obtain some money, if they see fit to do it in this way.
The fact that we are prepared to vote for this measure in principle, although we do not agree with the details, follows the perfectly proper and usual course. We wish to make it quite clear that we are continuing to place our urgent request before the government that they recognize the need for something quite separate from this, something much more flexible, and something which will make cash readily available to the farmers by payments in cash on their quota books for farm-stored grain.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I wish to ask a supplementary question of the minister. In answer to the hon. member for Eglinton the minister said that the money borrowed would be free from any condition of any kind. Does that mean it would not be competent for the bank and the borrower to enter into any arrangement they might see fit between them specifying the use of the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we are talking about money that is borrowed under government guarantee. Much more money has been borrowed without the government guarantee than with it. I think the total loans granted on the prairies outside the government guarantee are about $70 million, and under the guarantee about $7 million. These guaranteed loans are intended to make provision for the man who has not established a credit at the bank, and whose resources are not such as to warrant the bank in giving him a loan without some endorsement. There are about 8,000 farmers who have borrowed under the guaranteed provisions as at the end of December, and they have borrowed about $7 million. These farmers are entitled to the money, to obtain the cash, and we presume they use it for a useful purpose; but the banks have no instructions from the government that the money is to be applied in any particular way.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What limit, if any, is the bill going to put upon the amount available?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The amount is $1,500 per individual loan, and a total of $50 million.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say one word, since the position of the other two parties on this side of the house has been placed before you. We intend to vote against this measure, not because we wish to deny to the farmers of the west any small amount that they may get under this legislation. I recommend this consideration to my hon. friends of the other two parties in the house because, if this house votes in favour of the legislation, it will have placed its approval on all that the government intends to do. That is the reason we are voting against it. We are not going to vote for a measure which is inadequate, insufficient, and which means that the government proposes to do nothing more in this important matter than this particular resolution indicates.
We are making our protest in the only way in which members of parliament can make their protest. We are making a protest by our vote.
I should like to say one further word. My colleagues have endeavoured to discuss this measure, not with an idea of obstruction. May I say to my hon. friends on the opposite side of the house that the government makes its decisions. speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February S, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) - Mr. Applewhaite in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure for the payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves owned by the Canadian wheat board in respect of board stocks of wheat in excess of one hundred and seventy-eight million bushels at the commencement of a crop year, such payment to be made to the board by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Hon. members of this group approve of the resolution and for that reason it will not be necessary to spend too much time in discussion so far as we are concerned.
As a matter of fact, we showed our approval of the resolution rather more dramatically a few days ago when a motion of the leader of this group was instrumental in bringing this resolution before the committee ahead of the one upon which we have just had a decision; however, it was not the desire of the government to have it otherwise and we had to wait until this moment.
The decision of the government, which will I think meet with unanimous approval, to provide a part of the storage costs on the carry-over of grain, that part which is considered to be over the normal carry-over, is something which will be welcomed by grain growers across the prairies. It is expressing a reply to the demands made by the various farm organizations and by various hon. members of this house in previous times.
I can recall that in many previous debates hon. members of this group have strongly advocated action in this direction, and I particularly recall the hon. member for Moose Mountain doing so in one of his speeches as far back as 1946.
And while we approve of the immediate abjective of this resolution, which we feel will be of some help at this time, I should [ike to say that there is a need for some long-:erm planning on this whole question of =rain carry-over. I do not feel that this is i one-time proposition; I feel that we are loing to be faced with grain carry-overs for nany years to come.
Various hon. members, including the Minis-;er of Agriculture, have stated in this house hat it is a good thing on any farm to have i carry-over of grain from one year to an-)ther because it indicates a form of stability 

and an insurance against crop failure. I tend to agree with the minister that it is good to have stocks of grain on any farm, and if this is true of the individual farm then it is certainly true of the nation as a whole.
We are a trading nation; we are a big exporter of grain. Many of the traditional customers of Canada for grain will be looking to Canada for many years to come for a steady and reliable supply of the various grains they require. Therefore it is a good thing for Canada to have available in stock a reasonable volume of grain for quick shipment whenever and wherever it is required. However, if the nation as a whole is going to carry stocks of grain, then I think this resolution in itself is an admission of the fact that it should not be carried at the expense of the grain producer.
Even after this proposed legislation is put into effect the farmers will, of course, still be carrying a large part of the cost of storing grain in the elevators and all the cost so far as storing it on their farms is concerned. But this is a step in the right direction in that it introduces a new principle. It introduces an admission by this parliament that at least part of the responsibility should be borne by the national treasury. I believe there is a need for some long-term planning in that direction.
We have heard a great deal about the various ways of financing agriculture, particularly grain. I believe that much of the discussion we have had in the last few days could have been avoided if more careful planning had been entered into some years ago. I believe the best form of cash for grain in the farmer's hands is that form whereby the wheat board is able to accept delivery of grain and pay the farmer his money and take full possession and responsibility for that grain. That is the ideal situation.
When we get to the point where we will not have restricted quotas) when we achieve a situation wherein there is no congestion of box car and elevator space and we are still able to produce and move large volumes of grain in this country, then we can say we have reached a stage of orderly marketing. Until we have planning which will result in such a situation, we can hardly say that we have reached a stage of orderly marketing in the full sense of the word.
I am not going into any detail at this time because the consensus of the committee is that we want to carry this as quickly as possible, but I do want to express the hope that this government or any future government will take into consideration plans under which the wheat board itself may have at its

disposal greater storage facilities; not necessarily terminal facilities only, although those are important, but there could also be off-terminal facilities apart altogether from the country elevator system.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce and any hon. member from the western provinces will agree with me when I say that country elevators were never intended to be a place to store grain. Primarily elevators were places where grain could be handled and delivered and where cars could be loaded, in order to get the grain moving as quickly as possible. It was for this reason they were designed. But in the last ten years or so they have been attempting to perform a double function. While trying to handle the grain as expeditiously as possible the elevators have also been faced with the responsibility of storing grain. We have seen annexes built to the various grain elevators all across the prairies and we have seen what the results have been. There has been deterioration of grain and congestion due to the storage of grain in the elevators which has created a bottleneck in the system of orderly marketing.
I therefore hope that at some time the government will give some consideration to longterm planning in order to provide well constructed storage facilities so that grain can be kept for a considerable length of time without deterioration, so that we shall have an ample supply of grain in storage, storage for which would become the responsibility of the nation so that as a nation we will be in a position at all times to serve our customers quickly and expeditiously when orders arrive. In this way the bottlenecks and congestion which have bedevilled the whole system of orderly marketing in the last ten-year period will be removed.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is one of the occasions when we can all be in agreement, in so far as the principle of this resolution is concerned. It has been supported by this party for a very considerable time and, indeed, a very strong campaign was raised in behalf of a measure such as is contemplated in this resolution by the farmers' union in ,the prairie provinces. The achievement of this resolution represents the carrying into effect by the government of the desires of all the farming community that to a great extent produces wheat.
One of the situations consequent on the tremendous amount of wheat in storage in this country in recent years has been the fact that the return to the farmer is reduced by approximately $144,000 a day, which represents the storage charges paid to the elevator and storage companies on the amount
Wheat
now in storage in the elevators. Indeed, the storage and elevator companies are securing returns today far greater than was the case before the wheat board was established. The figure of $144,000 a day is a tremendous one, and farmers generally have felt, having regard to the fact that the government has assumed the responsibility for marketing their wheat, they should not be required to pay the storage over and above a normal amount of carry-over.
Whilst we support this resolution, I wish to point out one thing. It does not, however, while meeting the long-term needs of the farmer, do what is so necessary today, namely, immediately place cash in the pockets of the farmer. When one considers the immense increase in wheat production in recent years in the world, one begins to wonder how this problem will be finally met. The average wheat production among the wheat producing countries of the world, up till 1951 from the end of the war, was about six billion bushels a year. That amount was increased during the three succeeding years to about seven billion bushels.
With the new economic offensive of the U.S.S.R., which in part comprehends the adding of many tens of millions of acres to the production of wheat, one begins to wonder how this problem will be met in the years ahead. For certainly, if the U.S.S.R. carries into effect in the next five years its threatened policy to increase production of wheat and field crops by some 75 million acres, the surpluses that will be piled up in the U.S.S.R. and those countries that are joined with the U.S.S.R. under the Warsaw pact will bring about even more serious problems in respect to surpluses in the years ahead.
However, as far as this resolution is concerned, it is a step in the right direction. It is generally approved by all farm organizations. It represents an attempt on the part of the government to meet a problem which has become increasingly more serious year by year as the extent of the surplus of wheat has increased. Knowing that it is desired, representing as it does the implementation of the view that we on this side of the house have expressed on many occasions, we are going to support the resolution.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we in this group support the general principle of the resolution. On the other hand, we believe that the storage and disposal of surpluses can be dealt with satisfactorily only on an international basis. Unfortunately, in the past, nations have refused to co-operate to the degree necessary to make this possible, and attempts that have been made by the food and agriculture

Wheat
organization to set up a world food board and an international commodity clearing house were blocked by the member nations of that organization. So internationally we have failed to deal with the question of surpluses, and today we find surpluses are still on the doorsteps of the nations that produce them.
One cannot help wondering what has happened to the ideals we heard so much about in the early post-war days. It was said that we should abolish want and poverty from the world and that never again should we agree to a policy of reducing and destroying production in the face of want. There is no question that farmers have made an excellent job of meeting the challenge of production. They have expanded their production to a point where there is today a very substantial reserve of wheat. However, at the same time, while those large reserves of food exist, 50 per cent of the population of the world is still hungry. One may well ask what is being done at the present time to get these large surpluses of food to the people who need them so badly. Internationally, as I say, we have done very little. What has been accomplished in that direction may be called a drop in the bucket. Today the United States is reducing its production and taking steps to bring about a reduction in wheat acreage. In Canada we are depending very largely upon crop failure to solve this problem. By that I mean this. To a very large extent the government is depending upon the normal channels of trade to sell the wheat. Therefore they would be able to sell only what is equivalent to a normal crop which, of course, will not reduce the surplus we have on hand. Therefore I say the success of the government's policy in reducing these surpluses will to a very large extent depend upon short crops or actual crop failure.
Of course, on the other hand, a change in trade policy would bring about a very substantial expansion of markets. I could not help noticing what the press reported Sir Anthony Eden as having said when he was in Ottawa a few days ago. I quote the report in the Ottawa Journal of February 7, 1956, headed, "Canada Must Buy More From U.K." It states:
At a time when Canada is anxious to sell more goods, especially surpluses of wheat and other foods, Sir Anthony gave a plain warning that this country must expect to buy more as well as sell more in the British market.
Further on Sir Anthony is reported as saying:
"Canada last year exported to Britain about twice as much as we sent you. We want trade to keep on growing but it is most important this unbalance is rectified." iMr. Quelch.]
I would especially draw that to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce because in the past, when I have time and again insisted upon the need to try to bring about a balance of trade between Canada and Great Britain, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has said, "That is nonsense. We cannot balance trade unilaterally; it has to be done on a multilateral basis". Here is the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom telling Canada in no uncertain way that if we want to sell more to Britain we have to be prepared to buy more from that country. We have suggested that as a sign of good faith we could very well accept sterling from Britain under the definite understanding that that sterling would be' used for the purchase of British goods. The minister has stated in the past that if we accept sterling under the understanding it will be spent in Britain there is no difference between that and accepting dollars. Let me point out there is all the difference in the world. When you accept sterling under the definite pledge that that sterling will be used to buy British goods it assures Britain a market for her goods. When you insist upon payment in dollars and then use those dollars to try to offset the imbalance in trade with the United States you are not expanding the sale of goods from Britain and you are not helping them in any way to balance their trade.
I think there is a mutual obligation between countries to do everything they can to bring about a greater balance of trade. Therefore I am suggesting that instead of depending so much upon short crops or crop failures to bring about a reduction of our surpluses we should take steps to try to bring about a better balance between the dollar area and the sterling area. In that way and that way alone can we hope to expand our sales to the sterling area.
I was very interested to note a press comment to the effect that the Minister of Agriculture was going to try very hard to sell more agricultural products to Britain. I hope he succeeds, but certainly in view of the statement made by the prime minister of England it does look as though he considers it is an obligation on the part of Canada to find ways and means first of all to expand Canada's imports from Great Britain, and until we are prepared to do that there seems to be little likelihood of our expanding our sales to Great Britain.
Therefore until we find ways and means of expanding our exports of farm products it looks as though further heavy crops will continue to expand our surpluses. Normal crops will in all probability leave the surpluses as they are. Crop failures alone will reduce

Wheat
the surpluses. I am wondering whether the government is justified in believing that short crops will come about and reduce the surpluses. I believe that in the future crops in Canada will in all probability stay above the long-term average.
Let me briefly refer to the history of farm production for the past 40 years or so. It will be recalled that some 30 or 40 years ago most of our agricultural cultivation was done by the horse and the plough. It used to be the common practice to start breaking the prairie in early June and then later to start summer fallowing, probably in the latter part of June or in July. By that time the weeds would have grown fairly high and the soil would have started to dry out. In many cases the weeds would have gone to seed. In that situation the only likelihood of getting a good crop was in the event of excessive rainfall the following year. If you had a normal crop year you would get a poor crop. If you had a dry year you would have a complete crop failure.
That was the situation we were faced with in those years. But since then the majority of farmers have bought tractors. The farms are now highly mechanized, so we find the majority of farmers are able to get over all their land by machine in the first week of June. Using the tiller, the cultivator, the rod weeder and the one-way discer, they are now able to cover 20 feet in a swath instead of the old practice of 3 or 4 feet with a plow. As I say, as a result of that practice they are able today to cultivate all their land by the end of the first week in June, and land cultivated in that way and kept under proper cultivation throughout the year has an excellent chance of raising a good crop in just a normal year, of raising an excellent crop if you have a good crop year, and of raising a fair crop even in the event of a very dry year.
In my part of the country even when we have a very dry year we expect to get around 15 bushels to the acre and yet in the past, in the days when we had to use the horse and plow, we were very lucky indeed in a dry year to get our seed back. Now we use combines and they are a great improvement in harvesting methods. A combine leaves a trash cover on top of the soil which helps to prevent soil drifting so there is not nearly the danger of having a crop blown out by wind that there was in the days when we used threshing machines.
Some members will say that a combine makes the land weedy, but we now have sprayers which make it possible for farmers to spray the crops while they are growing even though the land does become infested with weeds. By the use of the sprayer the
weeds can be destroyed while the crop is growing and weeds now are nothing like the menace they used to be in the old days.
Then there is a tremendous improvement in the varieties of wheat. We can greatly reduce the hazard from frost by using the early varieties that have been introduced^ We can greatly reduce the hazard of rust by using rust resistant varieties. We can greatly reduce the damage by sawfly by using varieties that are resistant to sawfly.
Some members will say: Yes, but you have forgotten the fact that the soil is becoming depleted and is not nearly as fertile as it used to be. Of course there is widespread use of fertilizers in the west so even though the land is becoming less productive that can be taken care of by the use of fertilizer. I know that some members may say: Well, if all you say is true the farmer should be able to produce wheat much more cheaply today than in the past, but every single thing I have mentioned means a cost to the farmer. Mechanization has been a heavy cost. The use of fertilizer is a heavy cost. The price of ,a combine is a heavy cost. Therefore, while it is true that the farmers have been able to reduce the danger of crop failure to a very large extent, the measures they have had to adopt have been costly measures and do not permit them to produce wheat at a lesser cost.
So I would say that if the government is going to depend upon short crops or crop failures to reduce the surplus of wheat they may very well be disappointed unless, of course, the crop failures are on a worldwide scale. One thing, however, is very certain. The farmers themselves will do everything in their power to prevent a crop failure. They want a federal farm policy that will encourage efficiency rather than having to depend upon short crops to remove the surpluses.
I was very glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce emphasized the importance of building up a substantial reserve of wheat and, furthermore, has acknowledged the responsibility of the nation to pay part of the carrying costs of that surplus. The need of a reserve is obvious when 50 per cent of the population of the world are hungry, but the surplus is due not only to heavy crops but to the failure to make wheat available to nations unable to procure their supplies through the normal channels of trade. Instead of depending upon crop failures to remove the surplus, we believe that we should bend our energies towards ways and means by which these surpluses may be made available to nations that are not able to obtain the food they desire through the normal channels of trade.

Wheat
The farm organizations have made a number of requests to the government regarding payment of storage and carrying charges. I think the majority of the farm organizations have asked the government to pay the storage and carrying charges on all wheat in storage in the elevators at the end of the crop year. This resolution does not go as far as that. It leaves the responsibility for 178 million bushels with the farmers, and the minister assumes that the cost of the carrying charges will not go much beyond $32 million owing to lack of storage facilities, he says. If, however, the crop continues to be heavy, is the government prepared to see that additional storage facilities are provided to take care of the increase in the surplus?
As reported at page 847 of Hansard the minister had this to say:
Therefore, the cost to the treasury this crop year will he about $32 million. What it will be in subsequent years will depend upon the level of board stocks, but it cannot go much above $32 million in any event because of the physical limits on storage capacity.
The question that immediately comes to my mind is this. What is going to happen if we do not have crop failures? If these heavy crops continue,-something which is quite a possibility-what is going to happen? When we had the second heavy crop we thought the third year would be sure to bring a short crop but we had another heavy crop. We have now had about four heavy crops. There is no assurance that we shall have a crop failure next year. As a matter of fact, conditions out west right now look to be quite encouraging. I think we all hope there will be another good crop. But if these good crops continue, what is going to happen to that wheat?
The minister says there is likely to be a limit of about $32 million on the cost of storage because there are not the storage facilities available to take more wheat. Then v/hat is going to happen to that wheat? It appears to me that there are two alternatives. Either we shall have to build more terminal elevators and country elevators-and I understand there is a real need for the rebuilding of some of the existing elevators-or on the other hand I think the government should take steps to encourage farmers to build more granaries on the farm by allowing them accelerated depreciation, then-and I think this is an important point-include the farm-stored wheat that is in excess of a normal carry-over along with the wheat in the elevators at the time the government pays the storage charge, and then deduct 178 million bushels from that amount. It seems to me

that that is quite a reasonable suggestion. I think the minister's suggestion that the farmers should be prepared to carry 178 million bushels in the country elevators and the terminal elevators is a reasonable one. Provided that the surplus wheat can be stored in the terminal elevators, that procedure would fairly well look after the situation. But from what the minister says I gather that there is no intention to increase the storage space in the elevators because he says that the charge to the government will not go much above $32 million. If large crops continue, that will mean that the farmers will be obliged to put the increased surplus in granaries on their farms. Hence, instead of having a normal carry-over, you will have far more than a normal carry-over on the farms. It therefore seems to me that a reasonable suggestion is to say that the excess carry-over on the farm should be added to the amount of wheat in storage at the end of the crop year and then 178 million should be deducted from that amount. Before the resolution carries I should like the minister to say whether he does not think that is a reasonable suggestion.
There is no question that this legislation is definitely a step in the right direction. However, it seems to me it has three main weaknesses. First of all, it ignores the heavy storage charges of two years ago. I think it was in 1953-54 that we had heavy storage charges. We feel that that matter should be brought into the operation of this act. I understand that the year 1954-55 is covered under this act. If I am wrong in that statement, perhaps the minister would correct me.
In the second place, we feel that this legislation ignores the abnormal carry-over on farms about which I have just been speaking. I think that excess carry-over should always be taken care of so that the excess carry-over on the farm can be added to the general carry-over and then 178 million bushels deducted from the total of those two.
In the third place, it ignores the fact that many farmers are obliged to hold the current quotas on the farm owing to the unsatisfactory distribution of box cars which in some localities results in the farmers not being able to deliver any wheat at all on the quota, others being able to deliver one bushel, others two bushels and others three. Just yesterday I received a letter saying that even up to then the farmers in a certain district have not been able to deliver any wheat on the one-bushel quota. All they have been able to deliver is the original three hundred bushels but so far they have not been able to deliver any more. But the minister states that at some points they have a three-bushel

quota. That seems to be an unfair situation. I am not suggesting that it is an easy one to govern. It is not an easy thing to have a fair allocation of box cars. I think the minister will agree that steps should be taken to remove that injustice by bringing back into operation the policy we had some years ago-I believe it was about 1948-under which the price of wheat was raised by one cent a month on the quota. That one cent a month would take care of the interest charges and would compensate those farmers who had not been able to deliver their wheat as compared with the farmers who were able to deliver a three-bushel quota. If that was done I believe much of the criticism would be removed as to the injustice that exists as between the farmer who has not been able to deliver any wheat and the farmer who can deliver three bushels because the farmer who was not able to deliver any wheat at all would be receiving one cent a bushel on each bushel that he should be able to deliver. In any event, I think a great deal of the inequity of the present situation would be removed. As I say, we are greatly pleased that this legislation is being introduced and we will support it. Before the resolution carries, however, I hope the minister will indicate what his reaction is to the idea that the excess carry-over of the farmers should be added to the general carry-over in the elevators and then 178 million deducted from that amount.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to rise at this time to support the resolution that is before the committee. In my opinion this is an extremely important resolution. By this resolution the government is taking a long step forward in its current wheat policy. I am sure the minister realizes the length of the steps he is taking or the distance he is going. I do not think that the $32 million- important as is that sum in this resolution- actually demonstrates the extent to which the government is going forward in its wheat policy. By accepting the principle that excess storage and carrying charges over a certain quantity of grain shall be paid by the national treasury, by continuing as I am hopeful it will the current initial price for wheat, the government is in fact accepting important responsibility for this large quantity of grain.
The minister has said that the existing storage facilities will limit the amount of the government's commitment in the future to something in the neighbourhood of $32 million. I do not think that statement is likely to be borne out. Certainly it will not be borne out unless there is a substantial change in wheat board policy and government policy as far as storing grain is concerned. I was pleased that the Canadian wheat board and
Wheat
the board of grain commissioners this last fall made it possible for many communities throughout the prairies to build large storage facilities, usually in the form of a quonset hut that, when emptied at some point in the future, could be used as a skating and curling rink. These quonset buildings, or rinks, are going up in one community after another. They will hold anywhere from 100,000 to 200,000 bushels of wheat.
The policy of the government as it is now before the house means this: It means that these buildings are leased to the elevator companies, the elevator companies pay storage that is paid for by the government through this policy to the community that owns the rink. The farmers in that area will be able to deliver from 100,000 to 200,000 additional bushels of grain, place it in the rink building and receive the initial payment with the government bearing the excess inventory and carrying charges when the crop year ends. That is one way of placing not just $32 million in the pockets of the farmers of the west, but a much larger sum of money because of the payment of the initial price by the wheat board and the expansion of storage facilities.
I should like to see this resolution extended. I see no reason why it should be confined to wheat only. We have large quantities of barley and oats in inventory at the end of the crop year. I can see no good reason why the provisions of this resolution, applying as they do now to wheat, should not be extended to cover oats and barley. I should like to see the 178 million bushel floor raised, and the provisions of this proposed bill extended, so that the grain in storage on farms may be covered by it. If the government would amend this resolution to allow storage and carrying charges to be made on off-site storage in excess of 178 million bushels, the government would be putting large sums of money in the pockets of the producers. It would not be difficult for the title to the grain in storage on the farms to be transferred to the elevator companies, the farmer to receive the initial price and the government to accept the cost of the carrying and storage charges.
If this legislation could be expanded at this session or at a later session it would remove, to a large extent, the need to discuss the subject that we were discussing in the previous debate for many days. I am underlining this provision to point out that the government, by this action, is taking a very important step forward in its wheat policy.
I want to associate myself with many of the remarks of the hon. member for Acadia, particularly those remarks having to do with the disposal of wheat in international markets.

Wheat
I agree with him that so long as the majority of the people in the world are hungry, at least nutritionally hungry, it should be possible for governments in this day and age to see that the surplus food in certain countries is moved to deficit countries so that the people needing that food can have it available.
I am sorry that over the years Canada has not supported the idea of an international commodity clearing house or the idea of an international food pool, but rather has said through the Minister of Agriculture at the United Nations that Canada, as well as other nations, should handle the disposal of surplus products on a national rather than an international basis. Some fantastic suggestions can be made following that line of argument. I feel that if the member nations of the United Nations would endeavour once again to form an international food pool and an international commodity clearing house, call it what you like, we would be able to obtain a solution to our surplus problem.
I see the Prime Minister in the house, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the cabinet. The members of the cabinet appear to be in good attendance at this time. The Minister of Agriculture is not in his seat, but I am sure he is away on important business. Tonight's Ottawa Journal has a report of an interview with the Minister of Agriculture and the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, Selwyn Lloyd, which has to do with the disposal of Canadian wheat. It says:
The Canadian minister had assured a Windsor meeting recently that he would discuss possible further sale of Canadian food products with Prime Minister Anthony Eden and Mr. Lloyd during their visit to Ottawa.
It was learned today that he had raised with Mr. Lloyd, as he had done once before with Sir Winston Churchill, the possibility of Canada encouraging immigration from the United Kingdom by giving some compensation.
This time, Mr. Gardiner suggested, that the valuation might be 1,000 bushels of Canadian wheat for each immigrant. When the wheat was sent to the United Kingdom, the federal treasury would pay the Canadian wheat board which supplied the grain an amount which would be approximately $1,500 at present wheat prices.
Mr. Gardiner's plan, not offered as a government proposal, is designed to achieve two purposes- adjust the imbalance of trade now running two to one in favour of Canada and increase the number of United Kingdom immigrants to Canada, 30,150 in 1955 compared to 44,593 in 1954.
Let no one think that this is not a very extensive suggestion because at $1,500 per immigrant in 1955 the wheat board would have received from the national treasury $45 million. I am all for more immigrants coming to Canada. I am all for more immigrants coming here from the United Kingdom. I do not see why the Minister of Agriculture

should confine his suggestion, as apparently he has done, to persons coming to Canada from the United Kingdom. He might have extended it perhaps to France. They may not need wheat, but they may have taken some surplus butter, pork or something else. Perhaps the policy might have been extended to Germany or to Italy. I should like to know from the government whether or not this policy has ever been discussed in the cabinet, whether the government is giving it serious consideration or whether it is just another figment of the very fertile imagination of the Minister of Agriculture.
