speechtext: How many bushels will the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration require for a Canadian baby?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
That is a very good question. We might like to hear him comment about it. If this policy could be extended to other nations, I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture is going to pay 1,000 bushels of wheat for each immigrant from each nation or is he going to vary the amount? I wonder what immigrants from France might be paid, or from West Germany or Italy. I think that shows just how bankrupt the Minister of Agriculture and the government are when it comes to dealing with this important question of the disposal of wheat.
Other suggestions have been made that the government might pay a good deal more attention to. I hold in my hand a publication issued by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. It is entitled "Wheat Policy for 1956". At this point I wish to congratulate the Saskatchewan wheat pool board of directors and all of those people who had anything to do with drawing up the Saskatchewan wheat pool's 1956 policy. As far as farm policy is concerned, this is an indication of new and forward thinking in the farm organizations. I want to read the program because I think it is of great importance. The first plank is: "Maintenance of the wheat board for grain marketing". I think that will assure the Minister of Trade and Commerce that in spite of the Saskatchewan wheat pool's advocacy of cash advances its No. 1 plank, its 1956 wheat policy, is maintenance of the wheat board for grain marketing. I might say I am sure the Saskatchewan wheat pool would be glad to see the wheat board legislation expanded to include all grains, to include rye and flax.
There may be some who think that because it has been difficult for farmers to market wheat during the last few months it is the fault of the wheat board, it is the fault of the system of orderly marketing. I do not think that is so at all. I have had criticism to make

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
of the wheat policy that is followed. No doubt I shall have criticism to make in the future, and I shall have criticism to make in this statement. But I do not think the difficulty in the selling of Canadian wheat is in any way the fault of the wheat board system of marketing grain or of the personnel of the wheat board. On the contrary, it can be attributed to international difficulties, currency difficulties and certain aspects of the government's trade policy.
It is true that farmers have been able to get rid of a substantial quantity of flax on the open market. Some may think that because they have been able to get rid of a substantial quantity of flax, by using the open market facilities, the open market is a superior method of marketing grain. Ask the prairie producers today who sold all their flax last fall before the large price increase what they think of the speculative market in flax, and they will tell you they do not like it. They would far rather have the wheat board handling flax so that the producers of flax, if they had the right, could deliver it to the wheat board and get in any crop year the same price for flax as other producers.
The price would be less.

The wheat board comes before the agricultural committee every year and demonstrates the efficiency of the wheat board method of marketing grain. I should like to see the hon. member for Winnipeg South on the agricultural committee to advance his ideas, whatever they might be, and I am sure they would be properly dealt with by the wheat board officials.
The wheat board system should be extended to the marketing of rye and flax. I go one step farther. I see no good reason why the wheat board should be using the facilities of the grain exchange in selling oats and barley.
The second plank is: "Renewal and expansion of the international wheat agreement." That is a further projection of orderly marketing, or of government responsibility in the marketing of wheat. The reason we are having difficulty in the marketing of grain today, in my opinion, is not the fact that we have orderly marketing, with the government taking some responsibility at home, but the fact that the government's responsibility very largely ceases to exist the moment the wheat board has control and ownership of the wheat. If we can obtain an international wheat agreement, with the United Kingdom in that agreement, then this further extension of government responsibility in the marketing of grain may make it possible for producers in Canada to sell larger quantities of grain at satisfactory prices.
Wheat
I should like to see the government do something more. I am hoping, as I say, that a new international wheat agreement, with satisfactory prices and satisfactory quantities, may be signed; but I wonder why the Canadian government itself should not sit down with the governments of other nations and enter into contracts for the sale of Canadian grain over a period of years. Why should not the Canadian government, through the wheat board, attempt to sell substantial quantities of Canadian wheat to importing nations at agreed-to prices over a period of years? Perhaps the government would be prepared to do that; but in order to make such a policy feasible and practical something else has to be done. Our government should stand prepared to enter into contracts, with nations that would take our wheat, for the purchase of the goods that those nations can produce and wish to sell.
The government prides itself on believing in the capitalist system, and so do the members of the Conservative party. As I have sat in this house over the years and have seen legislation promoted by the government, it has seemed essential and necessary for the government to accept ever greater and greater responsibilities for the welfare of the people of the nation. I expect that, in the future, governments of the world must of necessity accept greater and greater responsibility for the marketing of grain. In my opinion, the days of free trade in grain are over and done with. If we continue to tie our wheat policies to a so-called system of free trade on the international markets it will probably be as unsuccessful as tying our domestic sales of grain to the so-called free market at home, which, of course, is the Winnipeg grain exchange. We shall obtain a solution to our wheat problems and to our marketing problems when this government accepts a greater measure of responsibility for the marketing of such grain.
I know the government criticizes the policy adopted by the United States government. Even though we may criticize their policy, the United States government is able to sell larger quantities of food products on the markets of the world, and we would be selling less and less wheat if the Canadian government was not able at this time-and I am very pleased that it is able at this time-to enter into contracts for the sale of grain to countries behind the iron curtain. Because the United States government, under public law 480, stipulated that they could not sell food products to communist countries, Canada has been able to increase sales of Canadian wheat, butter and other commodities to those countries.

Wheat
In his message to congress President Eisenhower asked the United States congress to delete from public law 480, section 304. Section 304 is the section which makes it impossible for the United States government to sell food products to iron curtain countries. Therefore, the time remaining for the Canadian government to increase its sales to such countries may be growing shorter and shorter.
The attitude of the United States government, a republican government, is not to get out of sales of wheat on the international markets, but rather to increase the scope of such sales.
The third policy outlined by the Saskatchewan wheat pool is: "An initial price of $1.40 for the 1956-57 crop year". The fourth statement in its wheat policy:	The national
treasury to make up any difference between the final realized price on the sale of the present year's crop and the I.W.A. minimum of $1.55 per bushel. In my opinion that too is an extremely important plank in wheat pool policy. It is saying to the Canadian government that it is no longer prepared to accept a continuing drop in wheat prices paid to Canadian farmers but is asking the government to put under prices a floor that will be received by the producers although to obtain such a floor money may have to be paid from the national treasury.
Five: The government of Canada to assume the carrying charges on all grain in store in Canada at the end of each crop year. That plank is being implemented to some extent at this time.
Six: A price of $2.05 a bushel on wheat used for human consumption in Canada. If that were adopted it might have resulted in an increase of one cent per loaf in the price of bread and it may not have resulted even in that small increase.
Seven: Maintenance of an aggressive sales policy including the arrangements by the Canadian government of suitable credits for wheat buyers, the acceptance of sterling and other currencies and the participation in famine relief programs and the economic development of backward countries as a means of increasing potential markets for Canadian wheat.
The measure before the house this afternoon has a great deal to do with the size of the final payment for the 1954-55 wheat pool. When I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce recently when a final payment might be made, he said, "I cannot say anything about it; I cannot say anything about an interim and final payment until the grain storage bill has been approved." Well, we have the grain storage resolution before us

at the present time and we have already had the announcement that an interim payment of ten cents a bushel is to be paid on the higher grades of wheat. I have welcomed that announcement but I do believe that the time is here when the government should announce not just the interim payment but also the final payment, the total payment to be made on the 1954-55 wheat pool.
It used to be the policy that when a farmer delivered a load of grain in the fall he obtained his initial price. He could look for an interim payment the following February, about mid-winter, and a few months after the close of the crop year, and usually before Christmas, he could look for a final payment. This was a highly satisfactory operation as far as the producer was concerned.
However, in the last two or three years the interim and final payments have been delayed for longer and longer periods. The interim payment that was announced the other day is one year late; ordinarily, as I say, it is made in February of the current crop year. On this occasion it is announced in February of the year following the end of the crop year. If the final payment should be made as late as the interim payment, then the final payment will not be made for many months to come. I hope that is not the case. I hope the government will announce the final payment now.
The only argument against making these payments at regular times so the farmer can plan his business is the statement that we do not know when we will be able to sell the carry-over or whether the international price will go up or down and to state a final payment and to close out the crop year may mean that we are making a final payment that is too high or too low depending on the prices for which we are able to sell our grain in the next crop year.
I would suggest that when wheat is grown in a good year it is ordinarily to be marketed in the coming crop year and that the greatest amount of fairness and equity can be obtained if the crop year in which the grain is marketed is closed out; in other words, if the wheat pool is closed out at an early date, shortly after the end of the crop year, July 31, and it is closed out on the basis of the current price for wheat at that time. If the price of wheat should go down, then of course the payments for the next crop year will go down, but that will be on the current crop. I do not think a good argument can be made in favour of such long and continuous delays in making these final payments.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I have a few suggestions that I wish to repeat. I should

like to see this legislation made permanent. I should like to see it extended to barley and oats and to cover larger quantities of grain, and I should like to see it extended to grain on the farms. I should particularly like to see the government establish a floor price of $1.55 for wheat as was suggested by the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I do not think that is a sufficiently high price but certainly it is a minimum price. I believe the government should have the wheat pool accounts closed out at regular times and regular amounts of money should be paid based on the floor price I have suggested.
The government should continue to support the establishment of a new international wheat agreement and there should be an expansion of sales in the international markets in the way I have suggested.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the house has before it at the present time a resolution to bring in a bill that will provide for storage of wheat in Canada at the end of the crop year. This will in effect provide for storage costs on 178 million bushels of wheat.
I am sure all hon. members of this house will in a degree be happy that the government has at least awakened to the seriousness of the marketing situation in Canada. Personally, I feel that the provision for the storage of grain in Canada to be paid for out of the federal treasury is a matter which should have had attention by this house and by the government of Canada at a much earlier date.
Whilst we are very happy that the government is now bringing in this legislation, I do not feel for one minute that it meets the situation confronting Canadian agriculture. I might say that since 1945, when I first came to this house, I have advocated a policy which would embrace the principle of the ever-normal granary. Before I came to this house and since, I know many members of this party have endeavoured to convince the government that it had not launched an aggressive policy to meet the needs of Canadian agriculture. So this evening I desire to treat the problem from two points of view, namely the economic viewpoint as it affects Canada, and, rather briefly, the effect which

Wheat
aur own program may have on world politics and, indeed, on the whole free world.
It seems to me that the federal governments we have had in this country have never ;ome to grips with the problem of conservation. I feel that this measure may be perhaps, to some extent, an awakening to the need for conservation of our soil in this country because, in effect, it will make it possible for the people in the hazardous occupation af agriculture to have a small degree of assistance in respect to their occupation.
Agriculture, of course, is a very hazardous accupation. When the farmer sows his grain, be has no way of being assured that he will reap a harvest. He has to take the chance on all the hazards in connection with the growing of that crop. Anyone connected with agriculture will realize that these are varied and many. He has to depend upon good weather, the vagaries of nature, rust, insects, pests and weeds and everything connected with the growing of wheat. To date the agriculturists and the people who are producing wheat in this country have to a great measure met the challenge of modern methods of production. Today western agriculture is highly mechanized and highly scientific. We have found ways and means of producing targer crops. In order to grow bigger crops, we have also learnt how to cultivate new strains of grain, how to spray our crops in arder to eliminate weeds and, of course, with new varieties and new techniques of production, I think we have met the production problem.
The greatest problem facing the agricul-;urists and the farmers of the west is one af price. I feel that agriculture is in a pre-larious position. If any hon. member of this louse feels that the whole economy of this country is not closely dependent on the prosperity and the health of agriculture, he has aeen very badly misled. If we do not have i prosperous agricultural economy, or the 10 or 12 per cent of the people engaged in agriculture are not in a prosperous condition, It will affect the whole Canadian economy. Indeed, I recall that in 1945, when I came to this house, we saw a delegation come to this parliament building and meet some of the cabinet ministers. It was a labour delegation interested in the welfare of over 6,000 workers who were unemployed in the farm machinery industry.
So it is that we welcome this resolution today which proposes to pay storage on 178 million bushels of wheat at the end of the crop year. I would like to see this legislation made a permanent piece of legislation and a permanent policy for this country. I would like to see it extended so that it would
[Mr. McCullough (Moose Mountain) .1
include a greater amount of wheat and so that we would have a proper vision of the picture, so that, instead of a nominal 178 million bushels, all wheat in Canada would become the property of the people of Canada and be stored at the expense of the federal treasury. What I have in mind is the picture of an ever-normal granary where we would store, having produced the wheat, not only enough for our domestic consumption, which is around 70 million bushels per annum, but also sufficient to meet all the sales we can achieve and, indeed, in the years of plenty, so that we would store for the years of scarcity. This government is rather shortsighted when it cannot even read the biblical treatment of this subject, in which we are told that in Egypt in the years of plenty they stored for the years of scarcity. So I think we should ask this government at this time to take a second look at this legislation and include in the bill means by which this government would take over all the farm grain and, as the hon. member for Assini-boia indicated this afternoon, take over also coarse grains and barley that farmers may wish to deliver to the wheat board.
As I have already indicated, this is a step in the right direction. I welcome it on that basis, but I feel that some responsibility for this problem has been accepted at long last by the government simply because the government knows that agriculture today, in every phase, is in a precarious position-our livestock marketing, our hogs, our beef and our grain as well. I wish to speak particularly about the grain situation because that is what this measure deals with. I asked this government for a return showing the number of trade commissioners the government had sent to posts in various parts of the world. The return indicated that there were 85 trade commissioners at 54 posts abroad. I asked how many of these commissioners were appointed with exclusive instructions to sell Canadian wheat and I was astounded to learn that not one single trade commissioner had been posted for the express purpose of selling Canadian wheat. When agriculture is our primary industry I think there should be at least some trade commissioners posted abroad whose explicit and sole duty will be to sell Canadian wheat. If that had been done it is my opinion we would not need to be worrying today about how our farmers are going to get some cash in their pockets in order to carry on their business and pay their debts.
I have said something about the government waking up to the problem confronting agriculture in this country. I know now that in some measure the government is waking up to the depletion of our forest resources and is at long last realizing that we need

conservation in that regard, but very little, if anything, has been done with respect to soil conservation. In the last few years the farmer's income has been going down and his costs going up. He has been caught in a price squeeze. Because of this fact, the hit-or-miss policy applicable to agriculture and the vagaries of a system whereby he cannot tell from year to year what his income is going to be, he cannot launch upon a proper and wise soil conservation program in his farming operations. Neither can he follow proper land utilization. If a farmer is going to do these two things, namely, conserve the nutrient content of the soil and practise soil conservation measures so as to have the ultimate use of his land, he must know whether he is going to get a fair return when he engages in one type of production or another.
If we are fighting to try to preserve freedom, if we are trying to preserve those things in our democracy in which most of us believe, then I feel that this measure does not meet that need. Therefore I hope the government will reconsider it. If they do not do so at this session I hope that when they have made this first halting step they will see fit subsequently to bring in more adequate legislation to establish the ever-normal granary. For the benefit of the people of Canada and, indeed, to feed hungry people throughout the world, an ever-normal granary policy should be established in this country.
I should like to deal briefly with the effect that I think the program outlined in the resolution will have on the world picture. We are, I am sure, all interested in orderly marketing. The farmers of western Canada have endorsed such a policy and supported the Canadian wheat board for many years. We believe that the old type of marketing under the Winnipeg grain exchange was not in the interests of the western farmers and, indeed, was not in the interests of the Canadian people. When the members of the C.C.F. party come to this house and try to express the opinions of the western farmers I think we are doing a service to everyone in Canada regardless of their occupation. Whether a person lives in British Columbia or Nova Scotia their income and standard of living will be affected unless a fair deal is given to the people who work in that great breadbasket of western Canada to produce wheat to feed our people and for export. The government must wake up and see that from the point of view of trading our wheat and engaging in international commerce we should establish in this country a stock of grain on the basis of which we can enter into longterm agreements with other nations. I feel
Wheat
it is rather presumptuous on the part of the government to expect importing countries to enter into agreements with us on a long-term basis if the government and the country are not prepared to guarantee delivery of grain to these countries under such an agreement.
That has been the situation in the past. We have had no program. The onus and responsibility for growing the wheat and storing it has been placed entirely on the backs of the western farmers. I am happy that the government has seen fit to go at least this far. I think each and every one of us realizes that a tremendous fight is going on throughout the world. It is a fight of ideologies, a fight where the ideology that will catch the imagination of men's minds will be successful in the end. If we join with other countries to bring about an international food bank out of which we can help to feed hungry people throughout the world we will have done more for democracy and the freedom of the world than all the munitions of war we can ever hope to produce. I am very happy that here at least is the first faint beginning of that sort of thing.
I realize that in the international field you have to have international co-operation, but perhaps one reason why we have not been successful in that regard to date is that we have never been prepared to do it at home. I sometimes think that the government is more interested in trying to maintain something which is as dead as the dodo, namely, the capitalist system, the free enterprise system. There is very little free enterprise of any sort left. I could have brought into the house a whole stack of reports of investigations under the Combines Investigation Act which would have shown clearly that there is very little free enterprise left and that on the other hand there is collusion and price fixing so that free enterprise is pretty well removed from our country.
Getting back to the international picture and a world food bank, in the final analysis I believe food may well be the deciding factor with respect to whether we shall have a free world or a world enslaved. I am very happy to support the resolution.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I say a word or two in connection with the resolution I should like to refer to the announcement made by the Prime Minister before six o'clock and take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres on their elevation to the post of parliamentary assistant. I am sure I express the sentiments of all in the house when I say that the Prime Minister's choice was not only

Wheat
wise but meets with the approval of members on both sides of the house. I wish these two young members every success in their new and added responsibilities.
With respect to the resolution before us, I think it is certainly most gratifying, after what we have heard about wheat in the last few days, to hear such hon. members as the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Assiniboia say that the government has taken the right step in the right direction. The fact is that the government has been in power for the last 20 years, and the reason it has been in power that long and the reason it has the confidence of the people of Canada from coast to coast is that it has the knack and ability to take the right step in the right direction.
Everybody knows, including hon. members of the opposition, that Canada is fortunate to have a man of the calibre of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with the wheat problem at this time, a problem that is international in scope and similar to the one we had in the early thirties. We find that the wheat board has been successful in selling better than average crops in the last few years and at the same time maintaining a fairly high price level. As I say, when you compare that with the situation in the early thirties we find that in my part of the country the farmer was getting a price as low as 19 cents a bushel for his wheat. What the farmer wants is to have this type of policy pursued. He would sooner sell one bushel instead of two bushels for the same price, and keep the other bushel at home.
The wheat surplus problem is one which affects not only the western producer but the whole economy of Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce recognized this fact when he made this statement as reported at page 846 of Hansard:
At the present time, however, I think there is a broad measure of agreement that it is in the interests not only of wheat producers, but of the country as a whole, that the wheat board should follow an orderly policy in disposing of its large holdings and not resort to panic methods of selling or giving-away. The experience of the 1930's is too fresh in the memories of all of us for anyone o suggest that attempts should be made to clear the shelves at any price.
Then he goes on further and makes this statement:
This proposal may, therefore, be regarded as a contribution, and an essential contribution, to the stability of the wheat economy of the prairie provinces and an indirect contribution to the stability of the whole Canadian economy.
We find that to the farmer this means a matter of 15 cents a bushel on the surplus that is under consideration or a total of some $32 million which represents purchasing power

in the hands of the buyer. It is something which not only will help the western producer but will benefit our national economy as a whole.
The important point to remember about this proposed measure is that it is retroactive. However, I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It could easily happen-and we hope it will-that we have another bumper crop in western Canada this year. Of course, if we have another bumper crop we shall naturally be confronted with acute storage problems. I should like to offer this suggestion. While I do not think it will cope with the problem completely I think it will probably go a long way toward covering the situation.
During the last 2J years I believe storage facilities have been increased substantially, to the extent of some 40 million bushels. One of the reasons why that was done was the accelerated depreciation which has been offered to grain companies whereby they would be able to write off for income tax purposes in three years, I think it is,-I do not know whether it is three years or five years-the buildings they put up for the storage of grain. If we should be confronted with another bumper crop, I would suggest that possibly the same privilege could be granted to the farmer; that is, if the farmer had approved storage buildings, he also would be granted this accelerated depreciation whereby, for income tax purposes, he would be able to write off those buildings in a matter of three or five years. That is a suggestion which I humbly submit to the minister and which I would ask him to take into consideration.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise purely to correct what I think is a misunderstanding which at present stands on the record. The hon. member for Acadia this afternoon repeated what has often been said in this chamber, namely that we could greatly increase our sales to Britain if we were prepared to do what is called "taking sterling". My belief is that that is a complete misunderstanding. My belief is that the people of Britain will have no part of it. It is in fact, of course, nothing more or less than our lending the money to Britain. I believe they have made it perfectly clear that they do not want to do business in that way. I believe they have made it officially clear. If that is true, I think it is a pity to leave the record as it is. If I am correct, I should like the minister to confirm it. We have so many difficulties with regard to so many things that are uncertain and perplexing in the matter of international finance that it seems to me a great pity to add to them by using this phrase

"taking sterling" which, so far as I can make out, really means nothing at all. If that is so, then I think it would be desirable to have it on the record.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been asked to touch on one or two points referred to by other speakers, so perhaps I might make a few remarks to close this debate. I would call your attention to the fact that over the last several days we have been discussing the government's program for assisting the farmer to meet an unusual situation. We have been told that part of the program is terrible, unbelievable and names have been applied to it that are startling; and it has been said that the other part is wonderful. It is rather remarkable that someone would not have had wit enough to add them up, strike an average and say that perhaps between the two resolutions they are not too bad.

My hon. friend did not. My hon. friend's picture of the prairie farmer is of a man with a tin cup looking for handouts. I think that is a most atrocious picture of western Canada. I may say that I went out there in 1913 and have been there a great deal in the ensuing 42 years. I think I know as much about western Canada as does my hon. friend.
However, these two complementary pieces of legislation were arranged to meet the particular needs of the farmers. The first piece of legislation was designed to give the farmer immediate cash. This year, for the first time, we encountered a situation where all grain elevators were filled to capacity, country elevators were filled and the movement from farms was extremely slow. There is no doubt in the world that buyers of wheat held off as long as they dared in the hope that our price would break just as prices in other countries were breaking. Finally they decided that ours would not break, and so the normal wheat movement commenced. But there has been a period when it was important for many farmers to get bank accommodation. The larger farmers had no great trouble, of course. They were accustomed to using the banks. They had ample collateral. They needed no help from the government in order to obtain the cash they required. However, there is the half-section farmer to be considered, or the three-quarter section farmer or the young man who is just starting and who has never had a bank connection. These men, in the judgment of the government,
Wheat
needed help. We arranged that help by making an agreement with the banks that banks would issue loans up to $1,500 on the security of the farm-stored grain, with the proviso that, as soon as parliament would meet, the government would undertake to see that its guarantee was given to the banks for repayment of those loans. A great deal has been made of the rate of bank interest. According to what we have heard, that apparently is a back-breaker for the farmer. But what does it amount to? The average loan to date has been $800. I would think that the average period could not possibly exceed six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
If there is anything my hon. friend has not covered that has happened over the last five years, I cannot tell him what it was. However, the total payment of interest by the farmer on the average loan is about $20 and that, of course, is a crime. However, the resolution on the order paper immediately below the bank loan resolution meant at least 10 cents a bushel to the farmer on all the grain he will market in this crop year. Surely, there must be a balance struck and a sense of proportion kept in mind, when hon. members say that one is a calamity and the other is a very good idea.
Now, I have mentioned the reason for the first piece of legislation, so we go on to the second piece of legislation. Over the years the accumulated overages have put a burden on the farmer to the extent that he has been required to pay the carrying charges, which

Wheat
are made up of storage and interest, on a larger amount of grain than is normal, and that grain is held in government storage over a much longer period than normally. In normal times the carrying charges on wheat amount to about 7-5 to 10 cents a bushel, depending on the size of the crop. Last year they amounted to 16 cents a bushel, and this year they could amount to more than that.
Well, the government said, what can we do to restore that situation to normal? We tried to find a period that could be considered normal before the period when the surpluses began to accumulate. We took the 15 years prior to the big crop of 1951 and found the average of the carry-over in each of those years. We found that it worked out to 178 million bushels on the average, averaging good years and bad years. We said that that is normal for the farmer. If the farmer is only dealing with a carry-over of that amount he has a normal situation. But the carry-over this year was about 215 million bushels larger than that, so we said the government will take the 215 million bushels and assume the carrying charges on that amount of grain for the full year. This amounts to about $32 million dollars, which is a contribution by all the taxpayers of Canada to those producers who have an equity in that prairie grain.
When we speak of the government advances we must remember that the government has no money. It is the taxpayers of Canada who have the money. When we say the government is paying these carrying charges, it means that the taxpayers of Canada are relieving the owners of the grain of carrying charges to that extent.
There has been a great deal of talk about payment for storage on farms. Questions are asked as to why the government cannot pay carrying charges on grain stored on farms. Grain stored on farms does not belong to the government. The government takes the grain into storage and acquires ownership by paying an advance of $1.40 per bushel on that grain when it is delivered to a country elevator; it then becomes the government's grain. The grain on the farms belongs to the farmer, just as the cattle on the farms belong to the farmer. If there is open storage space, the farmer will deliver the grain and get his payment. Then, that grain belongs to the government. If he has cattle on his farm he can market them, provided the stockyards are not congested and are able to take his cattle. There is no difference between the two. While they are on the farm they belong to the farmer. There is no way in which the government can properly pay any charges on grain that does not belong to the government.

It has been said frequently here that in the United States grain in the farmer's bin is paid for by the government, but that is not true. I have the rules here, and they are rather long. I can assure hon. members that the government of the United States does not have anything to do with grain until it is delivered into the government's approved storage. We, in Canada, cannot have anything to do with the grain until it is delivered into the government's licensed storage. The two are practically the same.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: They are approved on the farm in the United States.

speechtext: The government of the United States devised a scheme involving steel tanks which they put on a man's farm, and under inspection the grain is delivered into these tanks for government account. It is measured, graded and becomes the property of the government in the government's own bin. Well, that is no different from putting it in a skating rink that has been licensed by the board of grain commissioners as a government granary. It is exactly the same principle. Some people assume that everything in the United States is free. Perhaps hon. members would be interested in seeing the charges that the farmer pays for putting the grain into approved storage on his own farm, the inspection fees and charges of that kind. Sometime later in the debate perhaps I can put on Hansard an outline of the United States system, and thus disabuse the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite who have been making statements about how it is done south of the border.

A great deal has been said about selling wheat. We believe in the wheat board system of marketing. Unfortunately, the whole wheat board does not know how to sell wheat. George Mclvor has only been selling wheat for the government since 1931, and the other members of the board have only been at it 10 to 15 years. They have been in every market in the world. They know ever buyer in the world. Nevertheless there are people opposite who can tell

them a great deal about how to market wheat; and what they should take in payment. We have heard the cliches such as the ever-normal granary and the world food bank. I should like to have someone get up and tell me how each of these works in practice.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture spoke against them.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Perhaps he did not know what they mean either. I am sure I do not. It is about as nebulous a subject as I have ever encountered. However, that is the great solution. We should be taking some kind of money that is not our own and not convertible into our own, and because there is a barter deal we would not look at if it were a money deal we should make a barter deal. We have heard all these things. Nevertheless, the wheat board marketing policy does not change. That is the one great value of the Canadian system. The wheat board goes on year after year doing business with the same customers in the same way. The customers know they can rely on the wheat board. They know a bargain made by the Canadian wheat board will be carried out and carried out exactly in the terms of the contract.
I feel, therefore, a great deal of the time of this chamber could be saved by people who theorize about how grain should be marketed in foreign capitals. I would not venture myself to advise the wheat board. I have only been associated with the grain trade for 42 years. I have worked for customers who deal in every grain exchange in the world, and I think I have been in most grain exchanges in the world. I believe I have some idea how wheat is sold in foreign markets.
We are told our trade commissioners do not deal exclusively in wheat. Well, as long as they deal with wheat and give it the time required, I do not know why they cannot spend a few hours selling some other Canadian product without great detriment to wheat selling.
We have said nothing about the agents of the board who are the wheat marketing agencies of the world. Every Canadian exporter is an authorized agent of the board, and all of the great international firms are also agents of the board. These firms have offices in every country that is a buyer of wheat. And yet we are told that we ought to hire bright young men from industry and send them out to sell wheat. That is very amusing indeed. I am afraid some people do not appreciate the humour of it.
I do not know that I need say any more. 1 think the government have put forward an attractive and realistic program for the
Wheat
western farmer. We have taken steps to restore the abnormal situation in this year back to normal. We have made bank funds immediately available where required, and we have relieved the farmers of the carrying charges that may be regarded as abnormal. I think the farmer believes that we have done a job for him, and I am not prepared to take the chit-chat which comes from the far corner about a situation of the farmer in western Canada; I know too many of them.

Oh, yes.
I was in a meeting a while ago, and there was a good deal of complaint from one man. He was taking a rather bitter view of things. I happened to come out of the meeting with him. I had a few blocks to go and he had a car. He asked me whether he could give me a lift and I said "yes". I said: "This is a good car you have". He said: "Yes, I just bought it this year; I like it very much". He said: "You know, I am doing rather better than I said I was in that meeting. All my life I have looked forward to the day when I would have my farm clear of debt and one crop in the bins ahead of the current market". He said: "For the first time in my life I have that, and no man can tell me 1 am in very bad shape". I think that is the true picture of western agriculture as it is today for the real western farmer.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just one comment to make in this discussion tonight. I have listened very carefully to the speakers who have spoken since eight o'clock, and I have been rather impressed with the tone and the amiability that have emerged from the last two previous speakers. Unfortunately, I cannot concur in the opinion that has been expressed by my worthy friend, the hon. member for Vegreville. He indicated that because some complimentary remarks had been made in reference to the resolution before the house, it was suggested that the farmers of western Canada were giving universal approval to everything that the government of Canada has done in regard to the present crisis in the marketing of our grain. I will say at least this much for the resolution before the house. It at last is a recognition by the government that the farm population is faced with a real emergency and a real financial crisis at this time.
In his remarks just concluded, the Minister of Trade and Commerce also suggested that notwithstanding the fact it has become necessary to take emergency action, as indicated in this resolution, namely, paying storage

Wheat
on wheat in surplus above 178 million bushels, everything in the farm economy is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.
I said I had just one comment to make. That comment arises from the direct contact I have had with a part of the agricultural district of western Canada. I refer to the southwestern part of Manitoba. It was my privilege on Tuesday evening to attend a widely representative gathering, and from comments I heard from farmers gathered together at that time, I can say that they would not at all concur in the optimistic note that has been struck by the two previous speakers in this discussion.
As a matter of fact, on Tuesday evening at the hour of ten o'clock, the television program that has become rather famous in Canada during the past two weeks was broadcast over the CKX television station in Brandon. As a result of the impact of that Citizen's Forum discussion, which dealt largely with the present crisis in our grain-marketing situation, I was approached by a representative group of citizens who voluntarily, on their own initiative, had subscribed a substantial sum of money to replace the television set that had been blasted in another incident that has become well known in this chamber, I believe. The earlier presentation of that program over the Winnipeg station had resulted in the reaction of a certain Manitoba farmer, which led him to try to shoot one of the characters on the television screen. Mr. Chairman, I am in the possession of a sum of money for a fund, if such a fund exists, to replace the television set of this noteworthy citizen. I understand the suggestion emanated from the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort that the opposition combine in an effort of this kind. If such an effort is already taking shape, I want to assure hon. members that I have a substantial donation voluntarily contributed as a part of the protest of the citizens of western Manitoba.
I support this resolution mainly because it is the first recognition by the government that a real problem faces our grain producers on the prairies; but as the Winnipeg Free Press said in a recent editorial:
_ The hard fact remains that the government intends to do no more than the absolute minimum to help prairie farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR PAYMENT OF CARRYING COSTS OF TEMPORARY EXCESS RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thought this resolution was going to be through by six o'clock, but after listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce I cannot allow it to pass.
I think the suggestion that the gentleman whom the Minister of Trade and Commerce happened to meet sometime ago, who was in
fMr. Dinsdale.l
the position of having his farm paid for, having a substantial amount of money, and driving a very good car, was a typical farmer, does a great injustice to the farmers of this country. I am not suggesting that what the minister said is not true. It would seem strange that if among the 600,000 farmers in Canada there would not be a few who drive good ears. I want ito tell the minister that his own department, in co-operation with the Department of National Revenue, presents figures that show that around 10 per cent of the farmers in Canada receive enough income to pay income tax, and roughly half of all the income taxes which are paid by all farmers in Canada are paid in Saskatchewan.
I hope you will not come to the conclusion that because half of the taxes paid by the farmers in Canada come from Saskatchewan we are rolling in wealth. It happens that the percentage of the farmers in Saskatchewan who pay taxes is higher than it is for the whole of Canada but when you consider that 80 per cent in Saskatchewan and 90 per cent in Canada are not getting enough money to pay taxes, I think it points up the minister's conclusion as being quite unfair. It is small wonder that the farmers in the prairie provinces are up in arms when responsible ministers like the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture give the impression that the prairie farmers are in the position of the gentleman who is driving a new car and has all this money put by.
I might say that I had four years farming while I was away from here. I was fortunate enough to belong to the group which is able to pay income tax. However, I want to warn the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of National Revenue that a great many farmers who have been paying income taxes are going to be claiming refunds on the income tax they have paid when you come to average out the amount for five years.
I could cite case after case of farmers who were in the position two or three years ago of being able to have new cars, with all their debts paid, money in the bank and victory bonds but who are now in the position of having had to dispose of their victory bonds and their visible assets are rapidly disappearing. The minister fails to tell the people of Canada that 96 per cent of the world's wheat is handled by organizations similar to the wheat board and that while Canada is one of the big exporters in the world it is the only major country which till today has not provided some sort of subsidy.
Although it is one-sided, the minister has information from the United States and he

stagedirection

I suggest to the minister that he read the speech which his colleague, the Minister of Finance, delivered in New York on November 1. I am sorry 1 do not have a copy with me but the Minister of Finance while in New York pointed out that the Canadian farmers are producing the best quality of wheat in the world, and that they are prepared to sell it in competition with any other wheat in the world; but they cannot be expected to sell in competition with heavily subsidized wheat or in the face of tariffs. An example would be France. I am sure I am quoting the minister correctly but I will have a copy of the speech here tomorrow and I shall deal with this subject at greater length, but that is roughly the point the minister was trying to make-

-that many of the people in Canada are in the position where they cannot do anything but produce wheat and it is unfair for them to have to try to compete in world markets with other producers whose vheat is subsidized.
The last time I discussed the matter I had on my desk some information regarding Uruguay. If I remember correctly, since embarking on a subsidy program, Uruguay has increased exports tenfold; and the minister says we cannot pay farmers for storing on the farm. In Uruguay the government subsidizes the difference between what they pay the farmers and the price at which they sell the wheat in the world market. The price at the beginning of the crop year is $2.51 a bushel and it goes up each month until it reaches $2.72, a difference of over 20 cents. Therefore the farmers are paid over 20 cents a bushel for keeping the grain on their farms from the time they harvest it until-

But sixty million bushels is ten times six million and Uruguay is coming into markets that have been ours, and I do not see how the Canadian farmer who has been forced to produce without any subsidy is going to be in a position to compete with farmers from the United States, Uruguay, Great Britain and 67509-66i

Sweden and from every major wheat-producing country in the world with their large subsidies.
As I mentioned yesterday, France has recently completed a sale to Poland of some 12 million bushels. The French treasury pays $1.01 a bushel and the farmers through contributions to their funds put up over 50 cents a bushel; and $1.61 a bushel is what the subsidy amounts to on every bushel of wheat from France that went into the world market last year. How can the Minister of Trade and Commerce go into the markets of Europe and sell Canadian wheat in competition with high quality wheat from France that carries a subsidy of $1.61 a bushel? I think the minister is doing a real disservice in not bringing to the attention of his colleagues in the cabinet the fact that we are in a new situation where 96 per cent of the world's wheat, as I have said, is being marketed by boards such as ours, and we have been trying to compete without some form of a support price.
The minister made some critical remarks regarding the suggestions which have come from this side of the house concerning the accepting of a partial payment in soft currency and accepting barter. The minister is very slow to move, but he is gradually accepting some suggestions. A year ago he did recommend to his cabinet that wheat be sold to Poland on time and that the government underwrite the insurance. That has been well received across the country and Poland has been well pleased with Canadian wheat according to the information we received from them. However, when Poland wanted to buy 200,000 tons recently the minister said, we will give them 100,000 tons. I submit we cannot increase our sales with that sort of public relations policy when France is prepared to take a chance on selling 200,000 tons of flour and 100,000 tons of wheat.
I think it is as plain as A.B.C. that if we are going to continue sales in the new markets we have to be prepared to accept goods from these markets. I hope the minister's department, in addition to having a staff to sell Canadian goods abroad, will be prepared to take the initiative and give leadership in Canada to find a means whereby we can get some Polish goods into the Canadian market. Saskatchewan farmers last year bought United States and British cement at high prices. Boats were coming into Churchill for grain and I think it would have been an easy matter to have arranged to have some cement come into Churchill for the prairie market when the boats were going to take out wheat.
Apparently Poland expects to buy from 40 million to 60 million bushels of wheat each

Wheat
year for the next ten years. They think that of the 4,000 million dollars' worth of imports we bring into Canada each year they might expect to have four or five million dollars' worth of their goods come in. If we will take four or five million dollars' worth of goods from them they are prepared to take fifteen million dollars' worth of wheat from us. These deals are not going to come about by chance. The minister's agents have had long experience in selling wheat, but up to this moment we have not had people going into our potential markets in an effort to find out what goods can be brought from those countries into our country. How can they be sold in Canada without disrupting our automobile industry, our textile industry and our other industries? Believe me, unless we are going to face this problem very soon we are going to lose out in some of the potential markets we have.
Now there is a final word I feel obliged to say. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture particularly deserve the criticism from the farm members of this house for their failure to present the plight of agriculture in all of Canada in its proper light. It is a great misfortune, when corporation profits are at an all-time high and when every sector of our economy is prosperous, that the minister refuses to recognize this. Consider the job he did during the war as minister of munitions, when a million dollars did not mean a thing to him, when $50 million to develop the synthetic rubber plant at Sarnia was provided with a snap of the fingers, when it was apparent that probably it would be a dead loss but the minister was not afraid to risk $50 million because we had lost our supply of natural rubber. But, when it comes to providing some sort of security for the 600,000 farm families in Canada, that is a different matter. When it comes to giving them some assurance for providing food for our own people and our neighbours in other parts of the world, then we get the sort of performance we have had tonight. He gives the impression that the wheat farmers are driving new automobiles, that they have money in the bank, that their land is free from debt, or if not it is their own fault. I could not allow this debate to end without challenging that incorrect picture of western agriculture.

It is only through the chance remarks-or possibly the quite deliberate remarks-of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I rise to take part in this debate. If I heard his words properly, he said that the reason for not paying storage on farm-stored grain was that it does not belong to elevators. Later on he went on to explain
tMr. Nicholson.]
that paying for cattle in advance would be the same as paying for farm-stored grain. I am not going to take any exception to what he had to say in that respect. I leave that to the farmers in the house or those who represent farming communities to explain their particular point of view with respect to that question.
However, the part that did intrigue me was the fact that the grain stored on farms does not belong to the elevators. I would say that is probably perfectly right. However, how does that tie in with the question that was asked by the hon. member for Cariboo on January 20 of the Prime Minister? He asked:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister, in view of the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday that ships are awaiting rail shipments of wheat, owing to shortage of box cars. Will the government reconsider the offer of assistance in the building of the Pacific Great Eastern railway, in view of the fact that this railway will shorten the haul from the Peace river area to tide water by half the distance, in other words, that one box car on the short haul will do the work of two?
That statement is possibly very true-I might say it is completely true-that with the building of the Pacific Great Eastern railway the farmers will require one box car instead of two to transport their grain to a Pacific coast terminal. The difference is caused by the fact that the haul is shorter. Knowing full well that the Pacific Great Eastern railway is going into the Peace river area and that its terminal in the north Vancouver area is practically complete at this time, I would urge very strongly that the government consider building a terminal elevator at the terminus of the Pacific Great Eastern railway in North Vancouver.
Further, may I point out to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the annual report of the port of New Westminster for the year 1953 indicates that in the year 1952 the number of bushels of grain sent out of that port was 9,633,733. That is practically 10 million bushels of grain. In 1953 that figure dropped to 8,571,058, according to the following year's report, and in 1954 it dropped to 5,448,714 bushels. We have there a terminal elevator that will house some 800,000 bushels of grain. We have all the facilities that are required. We have, as the Minister of Transport will recognize, one of the finest ports on the Pacific coast. We have all the rail lines leading into the area, and we could use more grain storage facilities for the very purpose of assisting those farmers in the west.
I am satisfied, as other members of this house must be, that the crops of today are not just an accident. They are not just bumper crops that occur from time to time,

as we are led to believe. Certainly it should be recognized by this time that whilst the crops have been somewhat above what we would ordinarily call normal for the past several years, there have been many extenuating circumstances in the past few years that have helped to make these crops continue to be well over the national average over the past 30 years. For that reason we shall require more storage space at all times. Therefore I would once again urge the government to examine the possibility of building a terminal elevator at the port of New Westminster and one at the terminus of the Pacific Great Eastern railway.

I have only one point to make before this resolution passes. This bill is going to cost the taxpayers of Canada $32 million. I know there are many hon. members from eastern Canada and the west who are not too enthusiastic about it. This is a good deal of money, and so I suppose they cannot be blamed. However, as a western prairie member, I find this legislation, which is going to give the western farmers $32 million, pretty easy to take. As a matter of fact, I think it can be justified because, certainly, the west is in very serious difficulties at the moment. So I appreciate the fact that the rest of Canada is going to give the west a helping hand at this time. Perhaps later on we can reciprocate.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain said this was only a "halting step". It is a $32 million halting step, and I think it is one that will be welcomed by most prairie farmers. I know there are many hon. members in this house from other parts of the nation who think that Saskatchewan members are always complaining and are never satisfied. Well, sometimes I wonder whether we do not tend to paint a picture which is perhaps too gloomy. Frequently I wonder whether too much complaining by prairie representatives, may not mean in the long run, that the province's well-being is harmed.
In any event, I want to assure the Minister of Trade and Commerce and members from the rest of Canada that most Saskatchewan farmers are independent, self-reliant, aggressive and like to stand on their own feet. They do want the opportunity of course to earn a decent living on their farms. I do not think the resolution is going to solve the farm crisis, but I do think that 99 [DOT] 9 per cent of the farmers in the three prairie provinces will welcome it.

Mr. Chairman, I only rise to make one comment with respect to a matter raised by the hon. member for New Westminster who referred to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said respecting
Wheat
the farmer's wheat on the farm being in exactly the same position as his cattle. He owns the cattle; they are on his farm. He owns the wheat; it is on his farm. I am sure that analysis will not go down with the farmers of western Canada, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that is not the whole truth.
It is true that the western farmer owns the wheat on his farm and owns the cattle on his farm but there is a difference between the two. The difference is just this, that he can go out and sell his cattle wherever he can get a buyer to buy them. He can go to the local packer. He can go to the city where there may be several packing houses. He can sell to other people and other interests if he wishes. But there is only one channel through which he can sell his wheat and that is the wheat board, which is going to take the wheat eventually anyway. That is where the difference lies. So the farmer says: Well, if the wheat board is going to take my wheat anyway why not give me a loan on it or why not even give me an advance payment? That will tide me over. They will have the wheat even though it is stored on my farm. That is the difference. I believe my point is well taken and I think the farmers will know that the minister has slightly erred in his analysis of the situation.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has prompted me to make some comment. He referred to members-I think he was addressing this group particularly-who have made a strong fight against bank loans and the resolution preceding the bill which will force farmers to pay interest to the banks if they want to get some money on their farm-stored grain. He says he feels that members should have a sense of proportion and I think admitted in his statement that it was a rather bad piece of legislation. I agree with him. It is very bad and it is repugnant to the western farmers. He goes on to say that in view of that bad piece of legislation he is now bringing in a good piece of legislation which we should be happy about and accept. Therefore I suppose he feels we should start patting the government on the back. To me, Mr. Chairman, it is just like taking a good egg and a bad egg, trying to make an omelet out of them and saying that you have a pretty fair omelet. I do not think it would be a very good omelet. I do not think we should necessarily accept a bad piece of legislation just because the government is proposing to bring in something that may be a little more acceptable to us.

Wheat
Certain members of the house, particularly on the Liberal side, have tried to indicate that this measure is going to be of some considerable aid to the western farmer. I would not have been prompted to rise if that had been true, but nothing could be further from the truth. The $30 million that is going to be spent will be spent in the interests of everybody in Canada. Members on the government side of the house are prone to get up and try to indicate that the farmers ask for handouts. I remember quite well the U.K. agreement under which the government shipped to Great Britain over a four-year period 160 million bushels of wheat for the first two years and 140 million bushels for the subsequent years at a price of $1.55 a bushel when the world price was much higher.
I quite agree that we had price controls in Canada, and no group in the country was more ready to accept price controls than Canadian farmers. Under the agreement with Great Britain there was a have-regard clause stating that the British government would have regard for the prevailing world price which would have some bearing on the settlement at the end of the four-year period. According to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other government spokesmen the British government met every responsibility under the have-regard clause. But what did this government do? They had $65 million in the kitty left over from a loan arrangement with Great Britain so they said: We will give this to the western farmers and maybe they will be content. There was no sense of justice or proportion as to what would have been fair recompense having regard to the position of the farmers during that period.
The minister says that this is not the government's money but is the people's money. Of course it is the people's money and it is the farmer's money too. During the war 60 million or 70 million bushels of wheat were consumed annually in Canada and under the policy that prevailed at that time the farmer only received $1.25 a bushel. In addition, he subsidized the Canadian consumer to the extent of over 70 cents a bushel on every bushel of wheat going into the making of bread in Canada. Therefore I say that if anyone has lost his sense of proportion it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That is all I intend to say now other than to say that I do not agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre when he tries to say that this is giving the farmer something. That is the word he used, "giving". This is not a handout to the farmer. This is a policy of good government for all the Canadian people.

Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 83, respecting the payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves owned by the Canadian wheat board.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Chairman, ithis act has now been in operation for many years. I think the sense of the committee is that it has well served the purpose for which it was intended. Although many conditions have

conspired to reduce the percentage of the population which is taking part in farming, nevertheless I think we all recognize the fact that agriculture is doubly important, first of all because of its material contribution-and I shall come back to that matter in a moment- and second, because of the fact that those who live on the land, those who have that steady and steadying influence in their lives, form an extremely important part of the population. I think it is undesirable when they shrink to a small percentage. As time goes on I hope there will be offsetting considerations. Of course, we cannot overlook the fact that a great deal of work that was formerly done on the farm is now done in the factory and that one man can now raise the food that it formerly took ten men to raise. Nevertheless I think a measure like this one, which is designed to assist those who are now in farming and, perhaps even more important, to induce other people to take to that profession, is an extremely important measure indeed.
The board has carried on in a sensible way. 1 think they have won confidence. Their losses have been small. When we are asked to extend their powers, to extend the amount of the loan and to extend the percentage which may be loaned, I think we may feel that we are giving these powers to men who over a period of many years, have shown that they are responsible and that they are entitled to be entrusted with these powers. There are certain questions of detail which one will wish to ask with regard to the administrative changes, changes in capitalization-there are special points with regard to fishermen's loans-and others. But as there will probably be other members of the committee who would like to make some general observations-some of them who are closer to the industry than I am personally-I shall content myself now with saying just what I have said, namely that I feel that this is a matter of great importance; that for nearly 30 years we have had experience with those who are managing it; and that the results are such as to make us wish to continue the powers so that in the future the act may, if possible, serve a more useful purpose than it has served in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I have had a lifelong interest in agricultural credit because I am a great believer in agricultural development, particularly at this time in the still pioneer sections of our country. I think experience proves the historic necessity for agricultural credit by means of low-interest, long-term loans if you are going to establish a sound agriculture in any country.
Canadian Farm Loan Act
I am particularly interested in this resolution because I notice that there is provision for an increase in the amount of loans, up to a maximum of $15,000, and that the resolution suggests that loans can be up to 65 per cent of the value of the farm concerned, However, I wish to offer a few suggestions, as a result of experience, and to make a few criticisms.
I quite agree with the hon. member whc spoke previously that during the past 30 years the record of the board has been good and that it has served a useful purpose so far as agricultural development in Canada is concerned. Before proceeding further, Mr. Chairman, I must make it clear that I represent a particular breed of farmers who are obliged to work 12 months a year, from 12 to 16 hours a day in order to make a modest living anc who are more acquainted with the axe, ths crosscut saw and the grub hoe than they art with the rubbertired tractor or the combine It is on behalf of that particular group ol farmers that I am speaking this evening.
My first criticism and suggestion with respect to the administration of the act woulc be that, as far as British Columbia is concerned-particularly owing to development! in the last 10 or 15 years-the administratior is somewhat centralized. We have a brand office in New Westminster. To this offici everyone is obliged to write and from thi; office all the officials are obliged to trave to all parts of British Columbia. I sugges that the board would be wise to consider thi establishment even on a modest scale, of oni or two branch offices in the interior am northern sections of the province. I think thi experience of the Veterans Land Act admini stration indicated that, for efficient service that procedure was necessary.
I think the present rather centralized ad ministration, having just one office in NeM Westminster in British Columbia, at time creates inconvenience to the applicants a well as unnecessary delay. On account of th fact that the staff are obliged to make thei headquarters at New Westminster-and I ar not blaming the staff-there is a tendency t lose contact with local conditions in variou parts of the province, and with farmers an' farmers' organizations directly interested i: the administration of this act. I also thin' there is a tendency on the part of those wh have to deal with the larger farms-such a those in the Fraser valley and other parts-because of their lack of local contact wit local conditions, to underestimate the oppor tunities that are provided for pioneer devel opment. Those opportunities abound in th
